problem.title: Festival Tickets
problem.statement: Nia has 58 dollars for a festival. Admission costs 16 dollars, and each ride ticket costs 7 dollars. What is the greatest number of whole ride tickets she can buy without spending more than 58 dollars?
hints: Find all allowed whole-number values before choosing the greatest one.

solutionSteps.title: Find the feasible values
solutionSteps.body: The budget gives 16 + 7t ≤ 58. Subtract 16 to get 7t ≤ 42, then divide by 7 to get t ≤ 6.

solutionSteps.title: Optimize and check
solutionSteps.body: Because t is a nonnegative whole number, 0 through 6 are feasible and the greatest is 6. Six tickets cost 58 dollars total; seven would cost 65 dollars.

validationMethods: inequality derivation: (58 - 16) / 7 = 6, so every feasible whole-number ticket count is at most 6
independent boundary audit: 16 + 7(6) = 58 is allowed while 16 + 7(7) = 65 is not; every listed smaller count is feasible
notes: The problem separates finding the feasible whole-number set from selecting its greatest member.

problem.title: Aquarium Jugs
problem.statement: An aquarium can safely hold at most 40 liters. It already contains 13 liters. Water is added in full 3-liter jugs. What is the greatest number of jugs that can be added safely?
hints: Check the boundary count and the next whole number.

solutionSteps.title: Choose and check the maximum
solutionSteps.body: Nine jugs give 13 + 27 = 40 liters, which is allowed. Ten jugs would give 43 liters, so 9 is greatest.

validationMethods: independent adjacent-value check: 9 jugs reaches 40 exactly and 10 reaches 43; all answer choices were evaluated

problem.title: A Negative Multiplier
problem.statement: What is the smallest integer x that satisfies -4x + 3 ≤ 19?
hints: Dividing an inequality by a negative reverses its direction.

solutionSteps.title: Preserve, then reverse
solutionSteps.body: Subtract 3 to get -4x ≤ 16. Dividing both sides by -4 reverses the inequality, so x ≥ -4.

solutionSteps.title: Choose and check the endpoint
solutionSteps.body: The smallest allowed integer is -4. Substitution gives -4(-4) + 3 = 19, so the endpoint is included.

validationMethods: symbolic derivation: -4x ≤ 16 becomes x ≥ -4 after division by -4
independent option substitution: -4 gives 19 and works; -5 and -6 give values above 19, while larger offered values work but are not smallest

problem.title: Qualifying Time
problem.statement: To qualify for a relay, a runner's time must be less than 52 seconds. If times are recorded as whole numbers of seconds, what is the greatest qualifying time?
hints: Translate “less than 52” with an open endpoint.
Use the whole-number condition before choosing the greatest value.

solutionSteps.title: Read the endpoint
solutionSteps.body: The condition is t < 52, so 52 itself is excluded.

solutionSteps.title: Use the recording rule
solutionSteps.body: Among whole-number times below 52, the greatest is 51 seconds.

validationMethods: order argument: the greatest integer strictly below 52 is 51
independent choice audit: 51 is below 52, 52 is excluded, larger choices fail, and smaller choices are not greatest

problem.title: Donation Boxes
problem.statement: A club has collected 37 books and wants at least 125. Each full donation box adds 11 books. What is the least number of full boxes the club needs?
hints: Find the least whole number at or above the bound.

solutionSteps.title: Optimize and check
solutionSteps.body: Eight boxes reach exactly 37 + 88 = 125 books. Seven reach only 114, so 8 is least.

validationMethods: independent adjacent-value check: 8 boxes reach 125 while 7 reach 114; all offered counts were audited

problem.title: Rectangle Under a Perimeter Limit
problem.statement: A rectangle has positive whole-number side lengths. Its length is 3 units more than its width, and its perimeter is at most 46 units. What is the greatest possible area?
hints: Let the width be w and the length be w + 3.
First find the greatest feasible width, then compute its area.

solutionSteps.title: Find the feasible widths
solutionSteps.body: The perimeter condition is 2w + 2(w + 3) ≤ 46. Thus 4w + 6 ≤ 46, so w ≤ 10.

solutionSteps.title: Optimize and check
solutionSteps.body: For positive widths, w(w + 3) increases as w increases, so use w = 10 and length 13. The area is 130, and the perimeter is 46.

validationMethods: constraint derivation: 2w + 2(w + 3) ≤ 46 gives positive integer widths 1 through 10 and boundary area 10 × 13 = 130
independent enumeration: areas w(w + 3) for w = 1,...,10 increase by 2w + 4 each step; w = 11 would have perimeter 50 and is infeasible
